answers.label: A
answers.working:
Water flows out only while the surface is above the hole, so the useful head starts at \(h_0 = 20 - 5 = 15\ \mathrm{cm} = 0.15\ \mathrm{m}\) and falls to zero.

By **Torricelli's law** the efflux speed is \(v = \sqrt{2gh}\). Continuity gives \(-A\,\dfrac{dh}{dt} = a\sqrt{2gh}\), where \(A\) is the area of the vessel and \(a\) that of the hole. Integrating from \(h_0\) to 0:

\(t = \dfrac{A}{a}\sqrt{\dfrac{2h_0}{g}}\).

Here \(\dfrac{A}{a} = \left(\dfrac{5\ \mathrm{cm}}{0.2\ \mathrm{cm}}\right)^2 = 625\) and, with \(g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\), \(\sqrt{2 \times 0.15/10} = \sqrt{0.03} = 0.173\ \mathrm{s}\).

So \(t = 625 \times 0.173 \approx 108\ \mathrm{s}\), which is 1 minute and 48 seconds (with \(g = 9.8\) it is about 109 s, still closest). So the answer is option (A).

The period of a simple pendulum does not depend on the mass of the bob, so both pendulums have the same period.

In an elevator accelerating downward with \(a = g/10\), the bob feels an **effective gravity** \(g_{\text{eff}} = g - a = 10 - 1 = 9\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\).

\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g_{\text{eff}}}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{9}} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \approx 2.1\ \mathrm{s}\).

Option (C), 1.9 s, is what you get by wrongly adding the acceleration (\(g_{\text{eff}} = 11\)). So the answer is option (B).

After one half-life the chance that a nucleus has survived is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\). Decay in the second half-life is independent of the first, so the chance of surviving two half-lives is \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{1}{4}\).

Equivalently, \(N/N_0 = (1/2)^{t/T_{1/2}} = (1/2)^2 = 0.25\). So the answer is option (D).

**Top loop:** \(6 = 8I_1\), so \(I_1 = 0.75\ \mathrm{A}\).

answers.working:
For a plane electromagnetic wave, \(\mathbf{E}\), \(\mathbf{B}\) and the direction of travel are mutually perpendicular, and \(\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}\) points along the direction of travel. With travel along \(\hat{z}\) and \(\mathbf{E}\) along \(\hat{x}\), the magnetic field must be along \(\hat{y}\) (since \(\hat{x} \times \hat{y} = \hat{z}\)).

The one firm requirement, \(\mathbf{B} \perp \mathbf{E}\), rules out every option with an \(\hat{x}\) part: (A), (C) and (D) all have \(\mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{x} \neq 0\). Only (B), \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\hat{y} + \hat{z})\), is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{E}\), and its \(\hat{y}\) part gives \(\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}\) a component along \(+\hat{z}\). So the answer is option (B).

Note: as printed, no option is exactly right. For a plane wave travelling along \(z\), \(\mathbf{B}\) has no \(z\) component, so the only fully correct direction is \(\hat{y}\) (or \(-\hat{y}\)), which is not offered.

The radius of a ring grows by **linear expansion**, and for an isotropic solid \(\alpha = \gamma/3 = 3.6 \times 10^{-5}/3 = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}\).

The radius must grow from 2.1 m to 2.121 m: \(\Delta R = 0.021\ \mathrm{m}\), so \(\dfrac{\Delta R}{R} = \dfrac{0.021}{2.1} = 0.01\).

\(\Delta T = \dfrac{\Delta R}{\alpha R} = \dfrac{0.01}{1.2 \times 10^{-5}} \approx 833\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\).

Using the volume coefficient directly would give the wrong 278 \(^\circ\mathrm{C}\) of option (C). So the answer is option (B).

answers.working:
The slide is frictionless, so all the potential energy at A becomes kinetic energy at B: \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgh\).

On the flat track, friction \(\mu mg\) does work \(\mu mg d\) until the object stops: \(\mu mg d = mgh\).

So \(d = \dfrac{h}{\mu} = \dfrac{5}{0.5} = 10\ \mathrm{m}\). The mass (100 g) cancels and is not needed. So the answer is option (C).

The wire's field at \(r = 3\ \mathrm{mm}\) is \(B_w = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 45}{3 \times 10^{-3}} = 3 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{T} = 3\ \mathrm{mT}\). It circles the wire, so it is perpendicular to the axis.

The two fields are at right angles: \(B = \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} = 5\ \mathrm{mT}\). Adding them directly (7 mT) or subtracting (1 mT) ignores their directions. So the answer is option (A).

answers.label: B
answers.value: The normal diode has thicker depletion region and Zener diode has higher electric field across the junction.
answers.working:
A **Zener diode** is made from heavily doped p and n regions. Heavy doping means the uncovered charge needed to set up the barrier sits in a very thin layer, so the depletion region is very thin.

The junction voltage is dropped across this thin layer, so the electric field \(E \approx V/d\) is very large (of the order of \(10^6\ \mathrm{V/m}\) or more). That strong field is what causes Zener breakdown at a low reverse voltage.

A normal diode is lightly doped, so it has the thicker depletion region and the weaker field. So the answer is option (B).

answers.value: p rises linearly from zero to a maximum, falls linearly through zero to a negative minimum, then rises linearly back to zero
answers.working:
Momentum is \(p = mv\), and a constant force (constant acceleration) makes \(p\) change linearly with time.

Going out: \(p\) rises linearly from zero, then falls linearly back to zero at the momentary stop. Coming back, the car moves the other way, so \(p\) is negative: it falls linearly from zero to a negative minimum, then rises linearly back to zero as the car stops at its starting point.

From the maximum to the negative minimum the force is the same constant backward force, so the line passes straight through zero. Graphs (A) and (D) never go negative, and (B) has an impossible sudden jump in momentum. So the answer is option (C).

Taking the target levels as \(n = 2\) and \(n = 4\): \(\dfrac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_4} = \dfrac{1 - 1/16}{1 - 1/4} = \dfrac{15/16}{3/4} = 1.25\). So the answer is option (C).

Note: as printed, "second and fourth excited states" strictly means \(n = 3\) and \(n = 5\), which gives \(\dfrac{24/25}{8/9} = 1.08\), not among the options. The options are built on levels \(n = 2\) and \(n = 4\).

answers.working:
Let the chain have length \(L\), mass per unit length \(\lambda\) and weight \(W = \lambda L g\). When a length \(x\) has landed, the top of the chain has fallen freely through \(x\), so it moves at \(v = \sqrt{2gx}\).

The scale feels two forces: the weight of the chain already on it, \(\lambda x g\), and the force needed to stop the links arriving, which is the rate of momentum delivered, \(\lambda v \cdot v = \lambda v^2 = 2\lambda g x\).

Reading \(= \lambda x g + 2\lambda x g = 3\lambda g x\), which is largest just as the last link lands (\(x = L\)): \(3W\).

Half of the maximum reading is \(1.5W\), so the customer pays for 1.5 times the true weight, that is **50%** more. So the answer is option (D).

answers.working:
At the nearest and farthest points the velocity is perpendicular to the radius, so the **angular momentum** is \(L = m v_{\max} r_{\min} = m v_{\min} r_{\max}\).

**Energy conservation** between these points: \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv_{\max}^2 - \dfrac{GM_s m}{r_{\min}} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_{\min}^2 - \dfrac{GM_s m}{r_{\max}}\).

Substituting \(v = L/(mr)\): \(\dfrac{L^2}{2m^2}\left(\dfrac{1}{r_{\min}^2} - \dfrac{1}{r_{\max}^2}\right) = GM_s\left(\dfrac{1}{r_{\min}} - \dfrac{1}{r_{\max}}\right)\).

Dividing by \(\dfrac{1}{r_{\min}} - \dfrac{1}{r_{\max}}\): \(\dfrac{L^2}{2m^2}\cdot\dfrac{r_{\max} + r_{\min}}{r_{\max} r_{\min}} = GM_s\), so \(L = \left[\dfrac{2GM_s m^2 r_{\max} r_{\min}}{r_{\max} + r_{\min}}\right]^{1/2}\).

A quick dimension check rules out (A) and (C), and for a circle (\(r_{\max} = r_{\min} = r\)) option (B) gives the correct \(m\sqrt{GM_s r}\) while (D) blows up. So the answer is option (B).

Put the foot of the taller post at the origin: the crow starts at \((0, 20)\) and ends at \((60, 10)\), and the grain is at \((x, 0)\).

Use the **mirror (reflection) trick**: the path from the grain to \((60, 10)\) has the same length as the path to the image point \((60, -10)\) below the ground. The total length is least when \((0, 20)\), the grain and \((60, -10)\) lie on one straight line.

That line falls 30 m over 60 m, so it reaches the ground where \(20 - \tfrac{30}{60}x = 0\), that is \(x = 40\ \mathrm{m}\). Equivalently, the two flight segments make equal angles with the ground: \(\tfrac{20}{x} = \tfrac{10}{60 - x}\) gives \(x = 40\). So the answer is option (C).
